title: CMA on digital markets: designations, deals and where action may still be needed
label: 20 October 2026 · CMA update on Digital Markets regime
summary: The Competition and Markets Authority updated the committee on progress under the digital markets regime. The CMA described recent announcements (a provisional Strategic Market Status proposal for Microsoft’s business software, progress on cloud switching, and a proposed requirement to give fair access to iPhone NFC), explained why it sometimes uses voluntary engagement rather than formal rules, and set out how it measures impact. The CMA defended its pace and resources while acknowledging hard choices about priorities and promising urgent follow-up on Meta’s new publisher terms.

chapters.title: What the CMA announced this week
chapters.takeaway: The CMA proposed a provisional SMS for Microsoft’s business software, updated progress on cloud switching, and consulted on requiring Apple to give fair NFC access.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Start by explaining the recent announcements: what did the CMA do in the last few days?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We made three related steps last Friday and one today. Friday: we proposed to designate Microsoft with Strategic Market Status for its business software ecosystem (five services covering many UK users).

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We also published an indicative road map for where we will look next to decide if conduct requirements are needed, and we updated on talks with Amazon and Microsoft to reduce switching costs and improve multicloud.

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: Today we launched a consultation proposing a conduct requirement on Apple to give fair access to iPhone NFC, covering both payment and non-payment uses and the fees and technical terms that developers face.

chapters.title: What the CMA has already done and why it sometimes negotiates rather than imposes rules
chapters.takeaway: The CMA has used both formal designations and quicker informal engagement to get changes, aiming for speed, proportionality and measurable impact.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Since January 2025, what are the CMA’s main achievements under the new digital markets regime?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: Priority one was implementation: designations for Google search and mobile, Apple mobile, and now a provisional Microsoft decision; several conduct requirements are already in place, and some world‑first measures for publishers were introduced.

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: We try a mix of formal and informal tools: formal requirements give legal force but take time; targeted engagement can deliver fast, concrete changes where appropriate.

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: Lessons: use a range of tools, value a flexible legal framework so rules can adapt, and keep a participative approach with stakeholders to find workable solutions quickly.

turns.speaker: Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge
turns.text: Why was there a delay launching the next SMS after search and mobile?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: We ran what were in practice three separate mobile investigations for Google and Apple; getting designations that are appeal-proof took resource and time. We also reconsidered whether to focus on cloud or a broader Microsoft business software ecosystem after Copilot emerged.

turns.speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
turns.text: Some critics say the CMA is missing the mark; how do you respond?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: We’ve moved quickly: multiple designations, conduct requirements and immediate changes via engagement—pace and impact matter, not fines alone.

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We balance three aims: manage harms, attack the core sources of market power, and open adjacent markets—so far we’re moving across all three, but it’s still early days.

chapters.title: Cloud and Microsoft: when voluntary fixes are enough and when designation is needed
chapters.takeaway: Cloud issues split into licensing (likely in Microsoft SMS), and egress/interoperability (where voluntary steps are being tested before deciding on formal action).

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which cloud concerns will the Microsoft investigation address, and when will you decide whether voluntary measures are enough?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: Cloud issues from our market study were: egress fees, interoperability, and cloud licensing. We’ve put licensing (Windows server and database software) in the Microsoft road map because it may restrict competitors to Azure.

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: Egress fees and some interoperability improvements have seen voluntary moves from Microsoft and Amazon—removals or reductions of fees and new interconnection products—but we’ll review progress in spring 2027.

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We’ll judge by outcome metrics—are customers switching more, is multicloud uptake rising, are the new processes being used—and if voluntary steps don’t deliver, we’ll consider formal designation and conduct requirements.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: How will you measure outcomes for app stores and other commitments, and when will you report?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We track input metrics (complaints, appeal outcomes, data‑use incidents, requests for interoperability) and outcome metrics (developer confidence, investment, market openness). Firms must report privately to us and publish public reports; we’ll comment on those over the coming months.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: And for technical portability, like Kubernetes containers?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We’re flagging container portability and security across clouds as two focus areas to reduce friction; these are practical engineering issues where incremental improvements matter.

chapters.title: Publishers, Meta, resources and political backing
chapters.takeaway: Publisher controls are starting to work but more data arrives in December and March; the CMA will urgently probe Meta’s content‑use terms and insists it has government backing to use its powers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: You promised to monitor whether publisher controls strengthen publishers' bargaining with Google—what's changed so far?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: Google rolled out new tools after the June requirement; publishers now have more control and early signals show more deal activity. Critical data arrives 3 December (click‑throughs) and page‑level controls come in 3 March—those will clarify the value exchange.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: Meta says it will copy publishers’ sites under new terms from 30 October. Are you investigating and can you pause that deadline?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We only became aware publicly last week, we’ve written to Meta, and I meet them tomorrow to get details. We must understand the change before deciding whether to seek a pause or use enforcement powers.

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: We share publishers' concerns. We don’t have an SMS designation for Meta, so we’d consider other competition enforcement tools; we’ll act urgently on what we find from Meta.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: Were you aware Meta removed the word 'train' from its terms before last Thursday?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: Only after stakeholders raised it; we’re moving fast now to follow up.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: Has the Government’s strategic steer to support growth made the CMA softer on big tech?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: No. The steer asked us to be clear about pace and predictability; those principles match our approach. We still use legal tools when needed and chose priorities based on where UK businesses will get clear benefits.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: Would Government back robust action that might worry investors?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: I am confident Ministers back proportionate action that demonstrably benefits the UK economy; we must show the clear public interest in any strong step.

turns.speaker: Lord McNally
turns.text: Do you recruit from the big tech firms, and are there restrictions on moving between sides?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We do hire people with industry experience, and the CMA offers public-service appeals rather than private-sector pay; standard public-sector rules on conflicts and conduct apply to ensure independence.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: How do you make sure small developers and different-sized firms are heard?

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We actively consult and engage across sectors—publishers, app‑developers, fintechs, cloud customers—because their on‑the‑ground experiences shape priority choices and practical remedies.

turns.speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
turns.text: Do you have the technical skills to spot harms from personal AI agents and automated choices?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: Yes—we’ve invested in technical teams. For consumer‑facing agents the CMA expects existing consumer‑protection rules to apply and we’ve published guidance; if necessary, enforcement or designation tools remain available.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said you’ll follow up urgently on Meta and publishers—please send us that update. Any final point?

turns.speaker: Sarah Cardell
turns.text: We’ll follow up on Meta. Our approach is about using every tool—formal requirements, commitments and enforcement—selectively to get real, timely benefits for UK users and businesses.

turns.speaker: Will Hayter
turns.text: We’ll monitor the voluntary commitments closely, use outcome metrics, and we’ll not hesitate to move to formal powers if voluntary steps don’t produce the improvements we need.
